tasks.q: Write a program that puts six numbers into a grid of two rows and three columns.
brief: Read six whole numbers, one on each line.
The first three are row 0 and the last three are row 1.
Store them as a list of two lists.
Print the grid itself, the way Python prints it - for example: [[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]]
tasks.starter:
grid = []

# Read six numbers into two rows of three, then print grid

tests.why: Two sets of square brackets inside one. If you got [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6] you made one flat list instead of a list of lists.
The numbers fill the first row before the second - reading them down the columns would give [[9, 7, 5], [8, 6, 4]].
Build a fresh inner list for each row - reusing the same one leaves both rows pointing at the same three numbers.

tasks.fb: Make an empty row list, append three numbers to it, then append that row to the grid - and start a new row list for the next row.

tasks.q: Write a program that reports the size and contents of one tutor group taken from a list of lists.
brief: The list of groups is written for you - do not change it.
Read one whole number. It is a row number, counting from 0.
Print how many names are in that row.
Print that whole row on the next line, the way Python prints a list - for example: ['Jo']
tasks.starter:
groups = [['Ada', 'Bram', 'Cleo'],
          ['Dilan', 'Ella'],
          ['Faye', 'Gus', 'Hari', 'Isla'],
          ['Jo']]

# Read a row number, print how many names are in that row, then print the row

tests.why: Row 0 is the first row. Printing Dilan and Ella means you counted the rows from 1.
len(groups[r]) counts the names in one row; len(groups) would always give 4, the number of rows.
The rows here are different lengths, so the count has to come from the row you were asked about.
There are four rows, so 3 is the last row number - adding 1 would run off the end of the grid.

tasks.fb: groups is a list whose items are themselves lists, so len(groups) counts rows and len(groups[r]) counts the items in one row.

tasks.q: Write a program that prints the points a team scored in one round, from a grid of rows and columns.
brief: The grid is written for you - do not change it.
Each row is a team and each column is a round.
Read two whole numbers: the row number, then the column number. Both count from 0.
Print the value stored there, and nothing else.
tasks.starter:
points = [[4, 9, 2, 7],
          [8, 1, 6, 3],
          [5, 0, 12, 11],
          [10, 13, 14, 15]]

# Read a row number then a column number, and print the value there

tests.why: Row 0, column 0 is the very first value. If you printed 1 you took points[1][1], which means you counted both from 1.
The row comes first and the column second - points[3][1] would give 13 instead.
This is the previous test with the two numbers swapped, so it fails any program that reads the column before the row.
Row and column are the same number here, so only an index that is off by one will go wrong.
Four rows of four means the last value is at [3][3] - [4][4] is past the end of the grid.

tasks.fb: Two sets of brackets: the first picks the row out of the grid, the second picks an item out of that row.

tasks.q: Write a program that prints one whole row and one whole column of a grid.
brief: The grid is written for you - do not change it.
Read two whole numbers: a row number, then a column number. Both count from 0.
Print that whole row on one line, the values separated by a single space.
Print that whole column on the next line, the values separated by a single space, working down from the top.
tasks.starter:
table = [[3, 6, 1, 8],
         [5, 2, 9, 4],
         [7, 0, 11, 10]]

# Read a row number and a column number, then print that row and that column

tests.why: The row has four values and the column has three, because the grid is three rows of four - getting these the same length means you printed the row twice.
Row 2 is the last row and column 3 is the last column. Counting from 1 would crash or give the wrong line here.
A whole row is just table[r], but a column needs a loop that takes table[i][c] from every row in turn.

tasks.fb: A row is one item of the grid; a column is not stored anywhere, so you have to gather it one row at a time.

tasks.q: Write a program that reads six numbers and prints them back as a tidy grid of two rows.
brief: Read six whole numbers, one on each line.
The first three are row 0 and the last three are row 1.
Print the grid as two lines, one line for each row.
On each line put the three values separated by a single space.
Do not print any square brackets or commas.
tasks.starter:
grid = []

# Read six numbers into two rows of three, then print the grid tidily

tests.why: Two lines of three. Printing the grid itself would give the brackets and commas the brief rules out.
The rows stay separate even when the values repeat - a single print inside both loops would give six lines instead of two.
Build the whole line first and print it once, or use print(v, end=' ') and then an empty print at the end of each row.

tasks.fb: The outer loop is the rows and the inner loop is the values in one row - the line break belongs to the outer loop.

tasks.q: Write a program that reads nine numbers into a three by three grid and prints where each one is stored.
brief: Read nine whole numbers, one on each line, filling the grid row by row.
Go through every cell with two loops, using range(len(...)) for both.
For each cell print the row number, a space, the column number, a space, then the value.
Rows and columns count from 0. Work along row 0 first, then row 1, then row 2.
tasks.starter:
grid = []

# Read nine numbers into a 3 by 3 grid, then print the row, column and value of each cell

tests.why: The first line must be 0 0 1. If it says 1 1 1 you started both counts at 1 instead of 0.
With every value the same, only the positions change - this shows plainly that they run 0 to 2 in both directions.
Nine lines in total. Six or three means one of the loops is not running the full three times, or the print is in the wrong loop.

tasks.fb: The outer loop counts rows and the inner loop counts columns, so the inner one finishes once for every single step of the outer one.

tasks.q: Write a program that totals the merit points one class earned, from a grid of classes and weeks.
brief: The grid is written for you - do not change it.
Each row is a class and each column is a week.
Read one whole number. It is a row number, counting from 0.
Print the total of that row, and nothing else.
tasks.starter:
merits = [[2, 5, 3, 1],
          [4, 4, 0, 7],
          [6, 1, 2, 2],
          [0, 0, 9, 3],
          [8, 2, 1, 5]]

# Read a row number and print the total of that row

tests.why: Row 0 is 2, 5, 3, 1 which comes to 11. An answer of 15 is row 1, which means you counted the rows from 1.
There are five rows, so 4 is the last one - this is where counting from 1 runs off the end of the grid.
Zeros add nothing but the loop still has to visit them, so the total of 0, 0, 9, 3 is 12.
Total the four values in one row, not the first value of every row - that would give 20 whichever row you asked for.

tasks.fb: merits[r] is a single row, which is just an ordinary list - so a running total over it works exactly as it would for any list.

tasks.q: Write a program that reads a grid of three rows by four columns and totals every row, then everything.
brief: Read twelve whole numbers, one on each line, filling the grid row by row.
Print the total of each row, one on each line, starting with row 0.
Print the total of the whole grid on the last line.
tasks.starter:
grid = []

# Read twelve numbers into 3 rows of 4, print each row total, then the total of everything

tests.why: Three row totals and then the grand total, so four lines in all - forgetting the last line loses a mark even if the rows are right.
A row of zeros still prints its total of 0 - it must not be skipped.
If every row total is the same as the grand total you forgot to reset the row total back to 0 at the start of each row.

tasks.fb: Set the row total to 0 inside the outer loop, and keep a separate grand total outside it that never gets reset.

tasks.q: Write a program that totals one column of a sales grid.
brief: The grid is written for you - do not change it.
Each row is a day and each column is a shop.
Read one whole number. It is a column number, counting from 0.
Print the total of that column, and nothing else.
tasks.starter:
sales = [[3, 7, 2],
         [5, 1, 4],
         [0, 6, 8],
         [9, 2, 1]]

# Read a column number and print the total of that column

tests.why: Column 0 is 3, 5, 0, 9 which comes to 17. An answer of 12 means you totalled row 0 instead of column 0.
A column is gathered by taking sales[r][c] from every row - the column number stays the same while the row number changes.
There are three columns, so 2 is the last one - counting from 1 would ask for column 3 and crash.

tasks.fb: Loop over the rows with range(len(sales)) and keep the column number fixed - that is the one difference from totalling a row.

tasks.q: Write a program that reads a grid of four rows by three columns and totals every column, then everything.
brief: Read twelve whole numbers, one on each line, filling the grid row by row.
Print the total of each column, one on each line, starting with column 0.
Print the total of the whole grid on the last line.
tasks.starter:
grid = []

# Read twelve numbers into 4 rows of 3, print each column total, then the total of everything

tests.why: Three column totals then the grand total. Getting 6, 15, 24, 33 means you totalled the rows instead of the columns.
Only column 0 has anything in it - the other two still print a total of 0 rather than being skipped.
Here it is the last column that holds everything, so a loop that stops one column short would print 0, 0 and then the wrong grand total.

tasks.fb: For column totals the outer loop counts columns and the inner loop counts rows - the opposite way round to row totals.

tasks.q: Write a program that finds where a pupil sits in a seating plan and says how many pupils share that row.
brief: The seating plan is written for you - do not change it.
A seat holding the word empty has nobody in it.
Read one name.
If that name is somewhere in the plan, print its row number, a single space, then its column number. Both count from 0.
Then print, on the next line, how many seats in that same row are not empty.
If the name is not in the plan anywhere, print only: not seated
tasks.starter:
plan = [['Nia', 'Omar', 'empty', 'Pia'],
        ['Quin', 'empty', 'Rafi', 'Sol'],
        ['empty', 'Tam', 'Uma', 'empty'],
        ['Vik', 'Wren', 'Xan', 'Yves']]

# Read a name, find it in the plan, print its row and column and how many
# pupils are in that row - or print 'not seated'

tests.why: Nia is in the top left, which is row 0 column 0. Printing 1 1 means you counted rows and columns from 1.
Row first then column. Printing 2 1 means the two were the wrong way round.
Row 2 has two empty seats, so only two pupils are in it - the count must skip the word empty, not count every seat.
Yves is the very last seat in the plan, so a search that stops before the end of the last row will never find it.
A name that is nowhere in the plan prints that one line and nothing else - so the row and column must only be printed once you know the name was found.

tasks.fb: Two loops to search every cell, a remembered row and column that start at something impossible like -1, and then a separate loop over the found row to count the pupils.

tasks.q: The grid is [[4, 7, 2], [5, 1, 9]]. What does each piece of Python give back?
tasks.fb: The row index always comes first, and both indexes count from 0.

info.title: Rows first
info.text: A grid is described as rows by columns, so a 3 by 4 grid has 3 rows of 4 items each.

info.title: Two notations
info.text: Pseudocode in the exam writes a cell as array[1,2]. Python writes the same cell as grid[1][2].

info.title: One long line
info.text: Memory is one long line of addresses, so a grid is stored row after row. Reading along a row is the natural direction.

info.title: sum() a row
info.text: sum() totals a list, so sum(grid[0]) totals a whole row in one step - but a column still needs a loop.

info.title: Ragged grids
info.text: Nothing stops the rows being different lengths, though most tasks assume they match. Use len(grid[r]) if they might not.

info.title: Three dimensions
info.text: A list of grids is a three-dimensional array, which is how a program might hold a seating plan for every week of term.
